options.misconception: narrows the conference's work to commerce

answer.exemplar: The company was granted the right to make ordinances and to keep courts for the people living under its rule, while the sovereign kept authority in matters touching trade with outsiders and the title of land. options.text: It enlarges every holding equally, since the conversion factor applies uniformly across the sheet.
options.misconception: assumes one factor applies across the sheet

options.text: It makes the holding look larger or smaller than it is, depending on which survey its figure came from.
It leaves the holding unchanged, because a map records ground rather than shape.
options.misconception: thinks maps cannot alter apparent size

questions.explanation: A map turns surveyed ground into a size on the sheet, so apparent size depends on the survey behind each figure. Where surveys of different dates are mixed, holdings look bigger or smaller than they are.

options.misconception: expects a boycott to stop trade entirely

options.text: By the value of goods that left, since exports rising proves the sellers are inside the boycott.
options.misconception: confuses the boycott's target with the port's traffic

questions.topic: A clause replaced after a later war

questions.stem: Translator's note 47 asks for an account of why a clause agreed in one war was replaced after the next one.

answer.exemplar: Clauses negotiated in war are written to settle the disputes that war created, so they bind only while the settlement holds. A later war changes the military and political facts on which the clause rested, and the parties replace it either to remove an obligation that has become impossible or to record a new arrangement that the old clause cannot express.

questions.explanation: A clause made in one war carries that war's assumptions, so a later war can make it obsolete or impossible to honour. Replacing it records that the old arrangement no longer answers the new situation.
questions.hint: Ask which facts the clause depended on.

options.text: The promise depends on the losing party's good faith, since fault is a matter of intention.
options.misconception: makes good faith the test instead of fault

The promise depends on the local law of the place where the loss was suffered.
options.misconception: confuses the choice of law with the trigger

questions.explanation: The article conditions the duty to make good on fault being shown, and the choice of law tells only where the question is judged. Good faith and returned territory are background, not trigger.

questions.topic: A head-count target and a fee per head
questions.learningObjective: Design a method for measuring the cost of a head-count target
questions.stem: Translator's note 52 asks for a method by which the team can work out the real cost of a head-count target to a community.

answer.exemplar: Multiply the fee per head by the number of people the target allows, then compare that sum with the household incomes the returns describe and with the wages the same households could earn locally. The comparison shows whether the scheme is a tax on ordinary households, a subsidy to a minority who benefit from the departures, or a mixture of the two, and it must be made on the same period as the returns.

questions.explanation: The fee per head and the head count give a total burden, and only comparison with household income shows who bears it. Treating either as a bare figure leaves the effect on families unstated.
questions.hint: Compare the total with household income.

answer.exemplar: A customs return records what was shipped, by whom, and at what value, so it can be read for the effect of a refusal to buy. questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A company that kept its own court
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a company court fitted the wider system of justice
questions.stem: Translator's note 66 asks for a description of how a chartered company's court fitted into the wider system of justice.

answer.exemplar: The company's court sat for those living under the company's rule and applied ordinances the company itself made, including rules of property and of inheritance within the settlement. Its judgments were recognised by the sovereign's courts, which were the forum for offences against the crown's peace, for foreign trade, and for any case where the settlement's own rules were called into question.

questions.explanation: The company's court was a real forum with its own rules and recognised judgments, not a private scrawl and not a substitute for the sovereign's. It sat within a wider system, bounded by the charter.
questions.hint: Ask which forum heard what.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a map does to a family's fields
questions.learningObjective: Explain a gap between a map sheet and a county book

stimulus.body: A survey note records that the family in question held six acres by the county book, that the sheet shows a narrow strip of about one acre, and that the strip lies along the edge of the map where the surveyor's lines run close together. A later hand has written along the margin that the sheet there was filled in from an older plan of a smaller scale.

questions.stem: Translator's note 67 asks the team to explain the difference between the book and the sheet.

options.text: The family sold the difference, and the county book simply failed to record the sale.
options.misconception: invents a sale to explain the difference

options.text: The sheet was filled from an older smaller-scale plan, so it shrinks the holding the book records.
The sheet is the newer record, and the county book is a copy made from an earlier survey.
options.misconception: reverses which record is older

options.text: The lines run close together because the strip is narrow in reality, so the sheet is right.
options.misconception: accepts the drawn size as ground truth

questions.explanation: The margin note explains the gap: the sheet was completed from an older plan at a smaller scale, so the factor shrinks the strip. A sale or a narrow strip would need separate evidence.
questions.hint: Read the marginal annotation.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A head-count target and a fee per head
questions.learningObjective: Read a collector's statement of fee, cap and payment in goods

stimulus.body: The collector states that the sum of four pounds per head is payable on every person carried out of the island in the year, and that the number of such persons shall not exceed two thousand in that year. It adds that the sum may be discharged in goods at the market price of the day, and that the collector shall publish the count each quarter before the year closes.

questions.stem: Translator's note 68 asks the team to read the collector's statement and say what it sets up.

options.text: A fee for each person carried out, with no ceiling on the number in any year.
options.misconception: ignores the yearly ceiling entirely

options.text: A yearly ceiling of two thousand people, with the fee payable only on the last of them.
options.misconception: delays the fee to the final departure

options.text: A charge for each departure under a yearly ceiling, checked quarterly against a published count.
A payment in goods at a fixed price set by the crown, since the market price is only a guide.
options.misconception: turns a market price into a fixed price

questions.explanation: The scheme pairs a per-head charge with a yearly cap and adds quarterly reporting, so it is bounded and checkable. A charge without a cap, or a fixed official price, contradicts the text.
questions.hint: Ask how many things the statement fixes at once.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A boycott measured by a customs return
questions.learningObjective: Judge what a customs return proves and does not prove
questions.stem: Translator's note 69 asks the team to judge what a customs return can and cannot prove about a boycott.

options.text: It proves that the boycott was entirely successful, since the marked goods have all but vanished.
options.misconception: reads a fall in goods as total success

options.text: It proves that the boycott was entirely useless, since goods still arrived under other marks.
options.misconception: reads continued trade as total failure

options.text: It proves who among the houses intended to join, since the marks record the intention.
options.misconception: treats the marks as recording intent

options.text: It shows the effect on the named goods, provided it is compared with the same trade beforehand.

questions.explanation: A return gives quantities of the named goods over time, so it can measure a fall; it cannot grade success as total, or reveal intention. The comparison must be with the same trade earlier.
questions.hint: Ask what the return measured and against what.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A proclamation that turned status into a list
questions.learningObjective: Explain why listing a status changed what the state could do
questions.stem: Translator's note 70 asks why turning status into a list changed what the state could do with that status.

options.text: Because a list can be counted, checked and administered, which a general description could not.
Because a list settles who is superior, which a general description left in doubt.
options.misconception: assumes lists settle rank

options.text: Because a list ends the status, since the state no longer needs to describe it.
options.misconception: thinks listing abolishes the status

options.text: Because a list lets the state change the category at will each time it reviews the file.
options.misconception: assumes the list is meant to be amended freely

questions.explanation: A description tells officials who a category is; a list tells them which people and how many, which makes it administrable. It does not settle rank, end the status, or invite constant revision.
questions.hint: Ask what an official can now count.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A clause replaced after a later war
questions.learningObjective: Explain why war clauses fail in the next war
questions.stem: Translator's note 71 asks for an explanation of why clauses agreed in one war often fail in the next.

answer.exemplar: A clause negotiated in war is a settlement of the disputes that war produced, written in the light of the forces then in being. By the next war the map, the alliances and the balance of power have all changed, so the clause can promise something impossible, protect something no longer worth protecting, or leave untouched a question that has become urgent. Replacing it is simply an acknowledgement that the old terms no longer fit.

questions.explanation: Clauses carry the assumptions of the war that produced them, and a later war changes the facts underneath. The result is not bad faith but a mismatch between the terms and the situation they were made for.
questions.hint: Ask what the clause assumed about the world.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A promise that turns on a judgement of fault
questions.learningObjective: Say how a fault-based obligation operates in practice

stimulus.body: The clause provides that the party found to be responsible shall make good such loss as the other party shall have sustained, the amount to be assessed by three commissioners appointed by lot. It further provides that if the loss cannot be assessed in that way, the parties shall fall back upon the award of the neighbouring prince, whose decision shall be final.

questions.stem: Translator's note 72 asks the team to say how the obligation operates.

options.text: The obligation is fixed in advance by the clause, since the sum to be paid is already stated.
options.misconception: misses that no sum is stated

options.text: The obligation depends on the good faith of the party at fault, since assessment is a matter of honour.
options.misconception: makes assessment a question of honour

options.text: The obligation is triggered by a finding of responsibility and then measured by an agreed process.
The obligation lapses unless the neighbouring prince approves it, since his decision governs everything.
options.misconception: makes the prince's approval a precondition

questions.explanation: The clause names the trigger, responsibility, and the machinery for measuring the loss, with a fallback in the prince's award. No sum is fixed in advance.
questions.hint: Read the fallback provision.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A conference that set the rules and not the borders
questions.learningObjective: Say what a disclaimer of competence establishes

stimulus.body: The proceedings record the debate on the form of the minutes and on the method of choosing delegates, and close with the adoption of articles on the conduct of business. A separate paragraph, entered without discussion, states that nothing in the articles is to be taken as determining any question of boundary or of sovereignty.

questions.stem: Translator's note 73 asks the team to say what the proceedings establish about the conference's competence.

options.text: The conference claimed competence over frontiers, since it discussed sovereignty at the close.
options.misconception: infers competence from a recorded reservation

options.text: The conference set borders, since sovereignty was mentioned in its articles.
options.misconception: reads a mention of sovereignty as a settlement

options.text: The conference was dissolved, since a paragraph entered without discussion voids its work.
options.misconception: believes an undiscussed paragraph voids the work

options.text: The conference made rules while declaring itself unable to settle boundaries or sovereignty.

questions.explanation: The articles on the conduct of business were adopted, while the final paragraph disclaims competence over boundaries and sovereignty. That limits the conference's reach rather than enlarging it.
questions.hint: Ask what the closing paragraph refuses.

questions.topic: A company that kept its own court
questions.learningObjective: Weigh what a company court did and did not settle
questions.stem: Translator's note 74 asks the team to weigh what a chartered company's court did and did not settle in a distant settlement.

options.text: It settled local disputes between the company's subjects, while leaving wider questions to the sovereign.
It settled every dispute in the settlement, including those the sovereign had reserved.
options.misconception: extends local jurisdiction to reserved matters

options.text: It settled nothing, since a company had no right to sit in judgement at all.
options.misconception: denies the company's right to judge

options.text: It settled local disputes and quietly absorbed the sovereign's reserved powers as well.
options.misconception: claims the court absorbed reserved powers

questions.explanation: The company's court had real jurisdiction for local disputes over its own people, and the charter drew the line at what the sovereign kept. Denying it standing, or crediting it with absorbed powers, misstates this.

questions.topic: What a map does to a family's fields
questions.learningObjective: State what follows from a mismatch between sheet scale and survey scale
questions.stem: Translator's note 75 asks what follows when the scale of a sheet differs from the scale of the survey behind it.

options.text: The holdings shown on it are enlarged, since a smaller scale shows more ground per inch.
options.misconception: confuses small scale with magnification

options.text: The holdings shown on it are shrunk in proportion, so the sheet misstates their size.
The holdings shown on it are unaffected, because the factor cancels the difference in scale.
options.misconception: assumes the conversion factor cancels the scale

options.text: The holdings shown on it are unusable, so the sheet carries no weight as evidence.
options.misconception: condemns a sheet for a scaling error

questions.explanation: A sheet converts measured ground with a factor tied to its own scale, so a mismatch leaves the holdings drawn at the wrong size. The sheet remains evidence, but its figures need correcting.
questions.hint: Ask what the factor does to the measured ground.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A head-count target and a fee per head
questions.learningObjective: State what a head-count target and a fee per head amount to
questions.stem: Translator's note 76 asks for a plain statement of what a head-count target and a fee per head together amount to.

answer.exemplar: The head-count target fixes the largest number of people who may be moved out in a year, and the fee fixes the sum payable for each of them. Put together, they make movement a priced and limited thing: a household leaving has a charge attached to it, and the trade that carries people cannot exceed a stated number however much it might pay.

questions.explanation: One element caps the number, the other prices each instance, and together they shape the household's decision and the trader's planning. Reading only the cap or only the fee misses half.
questions.hint: Ask what each element limits or prices.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A boycott measured by a customs return
questions.learningObjective: Read what a comparison table shows about a boycott

stimulus.body: The table sets out the four goods named in the undertaking, and for each gives the quantity shipped in the previous year, the quantity shipped this year, and the names of the houses that shipped them. A footnote states that the previous year's figures were taken from the returns of the same port, and that the two years are not comparable because the second year includes goods that were previously stored in the bonded warehouse.

questions.stem: Translator's note 77 asks the team to say what the table shows about the boycott.

options.text: It shows a complete success, since every house in the trade now ships less than before.
options.misconception: reads less trade as complete success

options.text: It shows a failure, since the total shipped this year is higher than last year's.
options.misconception: uses the overall total to dismiss the boycott

options.text: It shows the boycott worked, since the named goods fell while other goods rose.
options.misconception: confuses other goods' rise with the effect

options.text: It shows a fall in the named goods, though the two years need adjusting before it is measured.

questions.explanation: The table gives quantities for the named goods across two years, the right measure, but the footnote warns the bases differ because of the bonded warehouse. That needs adjusting first.
questions.hint: Read the footnote on comparability.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A proclamation that turned status into a list
questions.learningObjective: Read what a register's rules show about status

stimulus.body: The register lists the names of persons entered, together with the district that supplied each name and the date of entry. A note at the head of the register states that no entry is made without an order from the capital, and that any person entered may be removed by the same order. The final column, headed removals, has never been used.

questions.stem: Translator's note 78 asks the team to say what the register shows.

options.text: It shows status held at the pleasure of the capital, since entry and removal both need its order.
It shows status granted for life, since the removals column has never been used.
options.misconception: reads an unused column as permanent grant

options.text: It shows a local decision, since each district supplied its own names and the register records them.
options.misconception: credits the districts with deciding the list

options.text: It shows a temporary measure, since the head note warns that the order may be withdrawn.
options.misconception: reads a caution about withdrawal as a fixed term

questions.explanation: Entry requires an order from the capital and removal the same, so the register records a status held at pleasure, not a fixed grant. An unused removals column shows only that none has been made.
questions.hint: Ask what authority each entry rests on.

questions.topic: A clause replaced after a later war
questions.learningObjective: Compare a replaced clause with one that survives
questions.stem: Translator's note 79 asks the team to compare a clause replaced after a later war with one that survives untouched.

options.text: The replaced clause shows that treaties are worthless, since anyone may discard them at will.
options.misconception: generalises from replacement to worthlessness

options.text: The replaced clause shows that a clause can outlive the facts it assumed, while the other still fits.
The replaced clause shows that the later war broke the treaty, while the other protects the parties still.
options.misconception: claims war breaks every treaty

options.text: The replaced clause shows that replacing a clause weakens the whole settlement of which it formed a part.
options.misconception: assumes replacement weakens the whole settlement

questions.explanation: Replacement responds to changed facts; it is not proof that promises mean nothing, nor that the whole settlement fails. A clause that survives still fits; one that is replaced does not.
questions.hint: Ask why the replacement was made.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A promise that turns on a judgement of fault
questions.learningObjective: State what follows when an obligation depends on fault
questions.stem: Translator's note 80 asks what follows when a promise's obligation is made to depend on fault.

options.text: The obligation arises whatever the parties later agree, since the fault is already fixed.
options.misconception: assumes the obligation outruns later agreement

options.text: The obligation disappears, since a condition that cannot be checked must be treated as unmet.
options.misconception: treats an unproven condition as fatal

options.text: The obligation waits on a finding of fault, and that finding fixes what must be done.
The obligation lies with the party who suffered the loss, since fault is the other party's affair.
options.misconception: puts the duty on the injured party

questions.explanation: A condition precedent means the duty arises only once the condition is satisfied, so the finding of fault triggers and measures the obligation. Assuming the duty already exists misreads that.
questions.hint: Ask when the duty comes into being.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A conference that set the rules and not the borders
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a conference can settle rules but not borders
questions.stem: Translator's note 81 asks for an explanation of why a conference is often able to settle rules while leaving borders alone.

answer.exemplar: Rules and borders pull in opposite directions for a conference. A rule about procedure can be agreed by states that disagree about everything else, because each state gets the same procedural footing and none loses territory by conceding it. A border, by contrast, must be drawn on the ground, and every state at the table has a claim upon the ground in question, so a border decided in a hall is a border imposed rather than accepted.

questions.explanation: Rules distribute procedure evenly, so states can agree them without conceding anything, while a border must be located and someone must feel the loss. That asymmetry explains the split.
questions.hint: Ask who loses by a border and by a rule.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A company that kept its own court
questions.learningObjective: Weigh what a charter and an ordinance book show together

stimulus.body: The charter grants the company the right to keep courts within its settlement and to make ordinances for the people there. The ordinance book contains rules of inheritance, of tenancy, and of the sale of land, each beginning with the words ordained by the company. A footnote states that offences against the crown's peace are tried before the crown's own justices, and that appeals from the company's court go to the privy council.

questions.stem: Translator's note 82 asks the team to weigh what the two documents together show.

options.text: A working local jurisdiction whose judgments were reviewed above, but whose worst cases went elsewhere.
A company that had taken over the crown's justice entirely, since the council only reviewed appeals.
options.misconception: treats appeal as evidence of total replacement

options.text: A settlement with no real law of its own, since every rule was made by the crown's council.
options.misconception: credits the council with making the rules

options.text: A company court that could try any case at all, since the exceptions were only formalities.
options.misconception: treats express exceptions as formalities

questions.explanation: The company made and applied local law, and its judgments were reviewed on appeal, but the gravest matters were reserved to the crown. That is a working local jurisdiction, not a takeover.
questions.hint: Ask which cases the crown kept.

questions.learningObjective: Read what a surveyor's letter establishes about a map's figures

stimulus.body: The letter tells the recipient that the sheet was reduced from a larger plan in order to fit the atlas, and that the reduction has been applied uniformly to every sheet in the volume. options.text: It establishes that every holding on the sheet is larger than the book records.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the reduction

options.text: It establishes that the sheet's holdings are drawn smaller, and that the books settle the true size.
It establishes that the reduction was applied unevenly, since the sheets disagree with each other.

options.text: It establishes that the sheet may be ignored entirely, since it was reduced to fit the atlas.
options.misconception: condemns the sheet for being reduced

questions.explanation: A uniform reduction shrinks every holding drawn on the sheet, and the letter directs the reader to the books where the two disagree. It describes neither uneven reduction nor a worthless sheet.

options.misconception: reads the whole return as the measure

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A proclamation that turned status into a list
questions.learningObjective: Account for how a list changed the lives of those it listed
questions.stem: Translator's note 86 asks for an account of how a proclamation that turned status into a list changed the lives of those it listed.

answer.exemplar: Before the proclamation, status rested on a description that officials applied as they saw fit, and a family could argue about what it meant. After it, a name on a register decided the question, a numbered token made the status visible when the holder travelled, and any entry could be removed by the same order that made it. Certainty and constraint arrived together.

questions.explanation: A register replaces argument with a record, giving the listed certainty about their standing, while the token and removal power make it conditional. Calling it a pure advance or a pure loss misses both halves.
questions.hint: Ask what certainty and what constraint came.

questions.topic: A clause replaced after a later war

stimulus.body: The earlier article bound the two states to keep the peace and to give no aid to each other's enemies. options.text: That the parties replaced the earlier article because it had been broken by the later war.
options.misconception: supplies a reason the text does not give

questions.explanation: The later article says it replaces the earlier in all its terms and continues until the parties agree to end it, which settles the relationship between them. Side-by-side operation goes beyond the text.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a map does to a family's fields
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a map does to the fields a family has farmed
questions.stem: Translator's note 91 asks for an explanation of what a map does to the fields a family has farmed.

answer.exemplar: A map does not show ground; it shows a figure drawn from ground that someone measured. The family that reads the sheet sees its holding as a shape whose size depends on the scale used and on the factor applied to convert the survey into the drawing. Where the survey behind the sheet was made at a different scale or a different date, the drawing and the ground part company, and the family's sense of what it owns changes with it.

questions.explanation: A map is a conversion, so the size on the sheet depends on the survey behind it, not on the ground. That is why the same field can look different on two sheets.
questions.hint: Ask what the sheet shows and what it measures.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A head-count target and a fee per head
questions.learningObjective: Say what a collector's statement provides

stimulus.body: The collector states that the sum of four pounds per head is payable on every person carried out of the island in the year, and that no more than two thousand persons may be so carried in that year. A table following the text sets out the four districts of the island with the number of persons carried from each in the previous year, and states that the figures were taken from the harbour books.

questions.stem: Translator's note 92 asks the team to say what the collector's statement provides.

options.text: A single fee per island, since the sum is charged once for the year rather than for each person.
options.misconception: reads the sum as an annual total

options.text: A ceiling with no charge attached, since the cap of two thousand makes the fee redundant.
options.misconception: treats the cap as making the fee redundant

options.text: Both a charge for each person carried out and a limit on the year's number.
A charge set by district, since the table shows the island divided into four charging areas.
options.misconception: reads districts as separate charging areas

questions.explanation: The statement has two elements, a sum per person carried out and a ceiling on the year's number; the table is evidence about usage, not a tariff. Reading the sum as an annual total misdescribes it.
questions.hint: Ask what the collector actually directs.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A boycott measured by a customs return
questions.learningObjective: Say what can be concluded about a boycott from a return

stimulus.body: The return lists goods shipped to four ports, with quantities and values, and a note at the foot states that the figures for the second port include goods that were re-exported from the first port within the same quarter. A second note records that houses shipping the three named goods had signed the undertaking, and that no other house had signed.

questions.stem: Translator's note 93 asks the team to say what can properly be concluded about the boycott.

options.text: The boycott stopped the named goods from leaving the island, since no such goods appear in the return.
options.misconception: claims the named goods stopped entirely

options.text: The boycott failed, since other goods continued to be shipped to the same ports.
options.misconception: uses other goods' traffic as the measure

options.text: The boycott cannot be measured, since re-exports make every figure in the return unreliable.
options.misconception: dismisses the whole return over one caveat

options.text: The return can measure a fall in the named goods, though the re-export caveat must be handled.

questions.explanation: The return gives quantities of named goods, the right basis for measuring a refusal to buy, and the note identifies the houses concerned. The re-export caveat needs handling, but does not void the return.
questions.hint: Ask which entries the note covers.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A proclamation that turned status into a list
questions.learningObjective: Compare a status fixed by proclamation with one fixed by custom
questions.stem: Translator's note 94 asks the team to compare a status fixed by proclamation with one fixed by custom.

options.text: The proclamation fixes status administratively and visibly, while custom leaves it to be argued case by case.
Both fix status in the same way, since a proclamation only records what custom already decided.
options.misconception: treats a proclamation as a mere record

options.text: Custom fixes status more securely, since custom outlives every proclamation made against it.
options.misconception: assumes custom always overrides a proclamation

options.text: Neither fixes status, since a proclamation is temporary and custom is only a habit.
options.misconception: dismisses both as ineffective

questions.explanation: A proclamation creates an entry, a register and a token, settling the question by administrative act; custom leaves it to be argued case by case. One makes status rigid; the other flexible.
questions.hint: Ask how each leaves a dispute to be settled.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A clause replaced after a later war
questions.learningObjective: State what follows when a war clause is replaced
questions.stem: Translator's note 95 asks what follows when a clause agreed in one war is replaced after a later one.

options.text: The earlier clause continues to bind the parties, since a clause is never withdrawn silently.
options.misconception: assumes clauses are never withdrawn

options.text: The later clause takes the place of the earlier one, which ceases to govern the same ground.
Both clauses bind at once, so the parties must satisfy the stricter of the two terms.
options.misconception: assumes both clauses bind together

options.text: The parties must now renegotiate everything, since a single replacement voids the whole settlement.
options.misconception: overstates replacement into voiding the whole

questions.explanation: A clause replaced in all its terms stops governing the ground it covered; the replacement carries the obligation instead. It does not survive alongside, and one replacement does not void a settlement.
questions.hint: Ask what the later clause says it does.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A promise that turns on a judgement of fault
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the structure of a fault-based promise
questions.stem: Translator's note 96 asks for an analysis of the promise whose obligation depends on a judgement of fault.

answer.exemplar: A promise of this kind is conditional in its origin and conditional in its measure: it does not obligate anyone until fault is established, and once established it fixes only what the finding requires. It therefore creates a procedure rather than a number, which is why such clauses tend to be written with forums, commissioners and standards of proof rather than with sums.

questions.explanation: The clause is conditional twice, in its trigger and in its measure, so it produces a procedure rather than a fixed amount. That is why it is written with forums and standards of proof instead of sums.
questions.hint: Ask whether the clause states a sum.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A conference that set the rules and not the borders
questions.learningObjective: Say what a conference journal shows about the meeting

stimulus.body: The journal records that the sitting was opened on the third day, that the order of business was agreed without division, and that a committee of seven was appointed to draft the articles. It notes that a proposal to consider the frontier question was withdrawn by its author before being put, and that the question was not discussed.

questions.stem: Translator's note 97 asks the team to say what the journal shows about the conference.

options.text: It shows the conference settled the frontier, since the question was withdrawn from debate.
options.misconception: reads withdrawal as settlement

options.text: It shows the conference achieved nothing, since no question survived the first sitting.
options.misconception: reads withdrawal as failure

options.text: It shows the conference was dominated by one state, since only seven members were appointed.
options.misconception: infers domination from a committee's size

options.text: It shows a conference that settled procedure and left the frontier question where it was.

questions.explanation: The journal records an agreed order of business and an appointed drafting committee, and that the frontier question was withdrawn rather than decided. Withdrawal leaves the question open.
questions.hint: Ask whether withdrawal decided anything.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A company that kept its own court
questions.learningObjective: Say what a regulation provides about the company's court

stimulus.body: The regulation states that the settlement shall be governed by ordinances made by the company, and that the company's court shall hear all causes arising among the inhabitants of the settlement. A proviso reserves to the crown the trial of treason and of offences against the king's peace, and provides that causes touching the goods of persons not resident in the settlement shall be heard by the company's court unless the crown directs otherwise.

questions.stem: Translator's note 98 asks the team to say what the regulation provides about the company's court.

options.text: It hears causes among the settlement's inhabitants, subject to the crown's reserved cases.
It hears nothing at all, since the proviso takes away the company's jurisdiction entirely.
options.misconception: reads a proviso as a total removal

options.text: It hears only causes about goods, since the proviso narrows the court to property disputes.
options.misconception: restricts the court to property disputes

options.text: It hears whatever the crown directs, since the crown may order the court to take any cause.
options.misconception: reads the direction clause as unlimited

questions.explanation: The regulation gives the company's court jurisdiction over causes among the inhabitants and names two cases reserved to the crown. A proviso carves exceptions out of a grant; it neither removes nor narrows that jurisdiction.
questions.hint: Ask what the proviso carves out.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a map does to a family's fields
questions.learningObjective: Set out how a family should treat a conflicting map figure
questions.stem: Translator's note 99 asks the team to set out how a family should treat a map that shows its fields at a different size from the county book.

options.text: It should prefer the map, since a map is the more recent and more pictorial record.
options.misconception: assumes maps are newer than books

options.text: It should treat the map as evidence of a scale, and take the measured extent from the book.
It should disregard both, since a difference of this kind shows the records are worthless.
options.misconception: condemns both records over a difference

options.text: It should claim the larger figure, since the family's title is best shown at its greatest size.
options.misconception: assumes the owner may pick the figure

questions.explanation: The map shows how the ground was rendered and the book records what was measured, so the measured extent governs. Choosing the larger figure substitutes preference for evidence.
questions.hint: Ask which record measures and which renders.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A head-count target and a fee per head
questions.learningObjective: State what a fee and a cap amount to for the port's treasury
questions.stem: Translator's note 100 asks what a head-count target and a fee per head amount to for the treasury of the port.

options.text: A fixed revenue, since the ceiling makes the income certain and the fee does the rest.
options.misconception: assumes the ceiling fixes the income

options.text: A fixed cost, since every person carried out costs the collector the same sum.
options.misconception: confuses the fee paid with a cost

options.text: A variable income capped at a known maximum, since the fee depends on how many leave.
No income at all, since the fee may be discharged in goods rather than money.
options.misconception: treats payment in goods as no revenue

questions.explanation: The fee per head makes revenue vary with the number carried out, and the cap fixes the ceiling. Fixed income, fixed cost, or no income because goods were taken each misread the arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask what varies and what is capped.
